title: Manual Checking and Verification
unit: CS-ICT251101 Monitor and Report Cyber Threats

parts.html:
At the end of this session, you should be able to:

  1. Check a detection yourself with its file hash, the console report and threat intelligence (PC 3.1).
  2. Check the action of the security solution in its logs and on the host (PC 3.2).
  3. Check security solution updates against the vendor bulletin and patch signatures as required (PC 3.3).
  4. Use the security solution to scan an infected system, following the update-then-full-scan procedure (PC 3.4).
  5. Record verified results and recognize failed actions that must be escalated.

Security consoles summarise. A good analyst checks the facts behind the summary: is the file really malicious, did the action really work, are the signatures really current, and is the infected computer really clean? Element 3 of the Competency Standards turns these checks into four performance criteria. In the lab you follow SOC-SOP-04 Manual Checking and Verification (~/day8/soc_verification_sop.txt).

A hash is a fingerprint of a file. SHA-256 turns any file into a 64-character code; change one byte and the code is completely different. Hashes let you check a detection without opening the file.

Step (SOC-SOP-04)HowResult
V1.1 Compute the hashsha256sum <file> (Linux)Get-FileHash <file> (Windows)
V1.2 Compare with the consoleDifferent = the file changed after the detectionVerdict: hash mismatch
V1.3 Look it upThreat intelligence list = verified maliciousVendor known-good list = false positive; neither = unknown, escalate
NOTE — Safe handling of samples
Never open, run or upload a suspicious file. Hashing reads the file without running it. In the lab the "samples" are harmless text files. In a real SOC, samples stay in a locked, isolated location, and only Tier 2 analyses them.

Microsoft Defender writes every action to its Operational event log. The event alone is not proof: check the host too.

Event IDMeaning
1116Malware detected
1117Action taken (Quarantine, Remove, Block)
1118Action failed (non-critical), e.g. file in use
1119Action failed (critical), e.g. access denied
1000 / 1001Scan started / finished
2000Security intelligence (signatures) updated
  • After Quarantine or Remove the file must be gone: Test-Path <file> returns False.
  • Event 1117 but the file is still there = NOT VERIFIED. Events 1118 / 1119 = FAILED.
  • Get-MpThreatDetection shows ActionSuccess (True/False) and ThreatStatusID (3 = quarantined, 102 = quarantine failed).
  • Not verified or failed actions are escalated to Tier 2 (Day 9, PC 4.3).

A security solution is only as good as its latest update. Compare three versions with the vendor bulletin:

VersionWhat It IsIf Older Than the Bulletin
Security intelligence (signatures)Descriptions of known threats; updated several times a dayOlder: update now with Update-MpSignature
EngineThe scanning program that uses the signaturesOlder: request the update from IT
PlatformThe Defender product itselfOlder: request the update from IT
TIP — Verify the patch
After Update-MpSignature, check Get-MpComputerStatus (AntivirusSignatureVersion) and the Defender event 2000. An update you did not verify is an update you only hope happened.

1. Update the signatures first, so the scan knows the newest threats.
  2. Run a FULL scan: Start-MpScan -ScanType FullScan. A quick scan only checks the usual hiding places (memory, startup, Temp).
  3. Verify what was found and what happened: Get-MpThreat, Get-MpThreatDetection, events 1001, 1116, 1117/1118, Test-Path.
  4. Record the result. A failed action is escalated (Day 9).

Why the order matters: in Demo 3 a quick scan with yesterday's signatures found nothing, while the same computer, updated and fully scanned, had a trojan in AppData\Roaming. "No threats found" only means "nothing this scan knew about, in the places it looked."

TermMeaning
Hash (SHA-256)A fixed-length fingerprint of a file; any change gives a different hash
Threat intelligenceLists of known-bad indicators (hashes, IPs, domains) shared by security teams and vendors
Known-good listHashes of genuine files published by their software vendor
VerificationChecking a result yourself with independent evidence
Signatures (security intelligence)The definitions the antivirus uses to recognise threats
Quick scan / full scanA scan of common hiding places / of every file on every drive
QuarantineMoving a malicious file to a locked place where it cannot run
Failed actionThe solution tried to act and could not: it must be escalated
